title: The Fed’s Playbook is Broken — Here’s What’s Next - Systematic Investor - Ep.360

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The Fed’s Playbook is Broken — Here’s What’s Next - Systematic Investor - Ep.360.docx

speakers: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
summary: Systematic Investor 360: data credibility after the BLS firing, Trump six-month macro scorecard (tariffs, immigration, Fed easing), Fed chair candidate Warsh, trend-following slump (WSJ article) and the AQR 'Diversifiers Forever' paper arguing trend suits long-term investors.

coverage.note: intro; BLS firing and TIPS implications
emerging-market comparison; survey response and revisions
Swiss tariff; Trump six-month scorecard begins
immigration and supply; Fed September cut
GDP measurement problems and data trust
Fed reform narrative and chair importance
Warsh implications for markets; critique points
hedge fund titans, central bank vs politician cycles; noise is signal
trend update, indices and sector P&L
WSJ article context on trend following
why hold non-correlated trend; boardroom pressure
cocoa anecdote; AQR Diversifiers Forever setup
AQR method and endowment payout logic; private equity leverage
nothing actionable: contrarian note and sign-off

completeness_estimate: 0.77 - the first reader captured the main threads (data credibility, macro scorecard, Warsh, trend slump, AQR paper); it skipped the Fed-reaction and savings-rate details, Warsh critique specifics, Man Group results and several caveats and sensitivity points.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: they are priced on the basis of the actual CPI print.
claims.claim: TIPS are priced on the actual CPI print, so tampering with BLS data (after the BLS head was fired) could raise the risk premium demanded in TIPS, though no meaningful reaction was seen.
claims.direction: higher TIPS risk premium on data-integrity fear

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: now we've got a developed market where they're firing the uh set decisions because they're not coming up with the right
claims.claim: Firing statisticians and weaker data credibility make the US look more like an emerging market, which could raise risk premia on US assets and affect inflation-indexed contracts.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: it's not that they've counted up to 200,000 jobs or whatever It's they they've done a survey and they've they come up with an estimate
claims.claim: Payrolls are survey-based statistical estimates with falling response rates (CPI imputation rising) and annual benchmark revisions, so revisions are partly mechanical, not necessarily political.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of the trade deficit that the US may have with Switzerland is actually due to gold
claims.claim: The 39% US tariff on Switzerland may overstate a trade deficit that largely reflects gold flows rather than goods trade.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: tariffs are are a tax increase
claims.claim: The first six months of Trump's policy produced a much slower economy than expected (tariff tax, consumer spending at about 1% annualized versus 2% normal), contrary to the run-it-hot expectation.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: we've seen a reduction on the supply side because of immigrants.
claims.claim: Immigration restrictions shrink labor supply, lowering trend growth to about 1% (from 2-2.5%) and meaning that wage pressure would reappear quickly if demand rebounds, which lowers the Fed's threshold for tightening.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: consensus now is that the Fed's going to ease in September.
claims.claim: Weak payrolls and negative revisions made a 25bp September cut near-certain, with a bigger cut possible if CPI did not rise.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: as systematic rules-based investors, of course, we don't care whether the numbers are right or wrong
claims.claim: GDP is mismeasured in a digital, services economy (unpaid self-checkout, influencers); systematic traders do not rely on the data, but other investors do, and GDP, production, income and employment sometimes diverge.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: the Fed's funds market which used to be the traditional kind of uh indicator of how tight or how um loose monetary policy was
claims.claim: Under ample reserves the fed funds market no longer signals the stance of policy, motivating Jeremy Siegel's call for Fed reform; the Fed is also criticised from both hard-money and easy-money sides.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: I think it is quite consequential. I mean, the Fed chair is hugely influential in setting the agenda.
claims.claim: The choice of the next Fed chair matters for the policy path because the chair sets the agenda, even with only one vote.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: He's very much uh in the kind of more of what you might call the hard money school.
claims.claim: Candidate Kevin Warsh is hard-money: opposes ongoing QE, favors lower rates on an AI productivity boom, and criticizes the Fed for facilitating fiscal profligacy; Fed cut 100bp in 2024 yet long yields rose 100bp.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: he could be a lot less favorable in the sense that if he's less in you know less inclined to do asset purchases
claims.claim: A Warsh-style Fed (monetary aggregates, credit growth, no asset purchases or bailouts) would be a radical departure and could be more challenging for equity markets if it finances neither the deficit nor markets.
claims.conditions: if Fed stops supporting deficit financing

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe at the moment actually it's the noise that generates the signal.
claims.claim: In a narrative-driven environment (as under Trump 1.0), the noise is the signal, which is hard for systematic models built to ignore noise and weakens trend returns.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: you go through cycles of strong central banks and weak politicians. We are in the reverse at the moment.
claims.claim: Central bank independence follows cycles; currently strong politicians and weak central banks, with hedge-fund titans influential in policy.

correction.issue: Speaker probably wrong: the remarks on strong politicians and weak central banks continue in the same run as the 'noise is the signal' point (credited to Niels), answering Alan's question 'nothing really surprises you with this administration, does it?'; no speaker labels, so moderate confidence.
correction.fix: Same claim, speaker probably Niels Kaastrup-Larsen: central bank independence follows long cycles; currently strong politicians and weak central banks.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer finished at 34 yesterday.
claims.claim: Trend barometer at 34 (weak) after the August 1 payroll shock and copper tariff reversals; CTA indices flat in early August (Beta 50 +5bp, -3.93% YTD; short-term traders -5.9%).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the recovery we've seen in equity markets have not been captured fully in terms of uh performance.
claims.claim: Trend followers cut equity exposure during the April drawdown and so captured little of the rebound; 2025 profits came from a few markets (gold, live cattle, soybean meal, grains short) with bonds and currencies difficult.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: clearly these um narrative quick uh market moves we've seen has not even been able to be captured by by shorterterm models
claims.claim: Short-term trend models struggled even more than longer-term models in 2025 on a vol-adjusted basis; longer-term trend was paid.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: this is only like the sixth down year so far since 1998.
claims.claim: The WSJ claim that trend following had its worst start since 1998 used an obscure index (Pivotal Path); trend has had only about six down years since 1998 and the late-1990s were positive, so the headline needs context.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: You've got these about turns on policy in relation to copper etc.
claims.claim: Trend following fails when markets are choppy; 10-year yields have been range-bound for three years and policy U-turns (copper) add chop.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: Is this, you know, is this the dark darkness before the dawn?
claims.claim: Negative press on CTAs (WSJ 2018, FT 2019) coincided with bottoms, so such articles may be contrarian indicators of the trend-following cycle.
claims.direction: long trend following after negative press

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: It's because it's non-correlated.
claims.claim: Trend is held for non-correlation, so during an equity bull run (+20%) a diversifier need not make money; the 1-5% allocation should not drive worry, though boardroom cycles make it hard to hold.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: you can't prove that something is broken it would reject that hypothesis.
claims.claim: After tough periods hold trend following based on a worldview that markets are inherently unstable and statistics cannot prove it broken; zero correlation means periods of losing while equities rise.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: long-term measures do change
claims.claim: Long-term performance measures are sensitive: the SG Trend 10-year return went from about +96% (June 2024) to about +30%; 10-year Sharpe 0.1, while the S&P is around 0.8, which drives allocator exits.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index 10-year return and Sharpe

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: narratives matter. You know, that's one of the points I said in narratives, stories more than statistics.
claims.claim: Allocators exit on narrative (careers, committee optics) after drawdowns of 15%, even when results are within statistical expectations.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that particular fund is down 57% or something like that this year.
claims.claim: Example: an oil trading firm that bought cocoa on an analyst's story while CTAs sold is down 57%, illustrating bad timing against trend.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: the downside of zero correlation.
claims.claim: Zero correlation means periods when equities are up and the diversifier loses; behavior, not return, is the issue (his LinkedIn piece 'highs and lows of allocating to trend following').

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: the idea is to maintain the real
claims.claim: AQR's 'Diversifiers Forever' analyses UK foundations (45% public equity, 20% private equity) back to 1972, adding trend as liquid diversifier to maintain real portfolio value while paying out about 5%.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: they discounted by 60% to reflect I guess that there's a surv survivorship bias
claims.claim: The AQR study backfills trend using the SG Trend index (adjusted), the HFRI Systematic Macro index (discounted 60% for survivorship) in the 1990s, and a hypothetical in-house system (discounted 60%) before 1990.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: a smoother ride means an average a higher average payout
claims.claim: A smoother return stream raises the average payout for a spending portfolio (endowment, retirement drawdown) because drawdowns during payouts erode capital; 10% allocation or 10% portable alpha improved return and Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: the real cost of debt has gone up from say 2.2% to um 4 a.5%
claims.claim: Higher real cost of debt (2.2% to 4.5%) cuts the leverage boost to private equity returns from about 4 points to 0.4 points, about 3.5% lower expected return.
claims.indicator: real cost of debt, private equity leverage boost

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Barkley long short equity index actually has an annual um correlation to a 60/40 portfolio
claims.claim: From 2000 to June 2025 Barclay long/short equity had a correlation of about 0.66 to a 60/40 portfolio, global macro 0.34, while the SG Trend Index was -0.38 and made money in most crises.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: adding 20% of one of these strategies compared to adding 20% of a say a sock and trend index.
claims.claim: Adding 20% trend gives the highest portfolio Sharpe improvement versus 20% of any Barclay hedge fund strategy; excluding the 1970s and 1980-2009 bull market the results still hold.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: I'm not hearing so many people say it now but you know the long-term characteristics of
claims.claim: Negative press may mark the bottom; long-term characteristics of trend following are unchanged.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: maybe in defense of Trump, you might say, well, maybe maybe a new approach is needed and maybe that's the point to to get more reliable stats.
claims.claim: Counterpoint: replacing BLS leadership could be a legitimate attempt to fix declining data quality (low survey response, imputation), so the firing is not proof of manipulation.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: And the savings rate has has increased since last year to about 4 and a.5% now. Um, you know, back in the late 2010s was more like 5 and a half 6%.
claims.claim: The US savings rate rose to about 4.5% (from lower) and may still rise toward the 5.5-6% of the late 2010s, a further drag on consumer spending already growing near 1%.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: there was hopes of kind of fiscal stimulus and the big beautiful bill etc we're not really seeing that that there might be a little bit of that next year
claims.claim: The expected pro-growth levers of the new administration (fiscal stimulus via the big beautiful bill, deregulation) have not shown up in the data, so only tariffs and immigration effects are visible; some stimulus may come in 2026.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: the economy re rebounded very strongly and that was largely driven by a surge of immigration into the US.
claims.claim: The 2023 US rebound was largely driven by a surge in immigration (labour supply), so reversing immigration reverses part of that growth driver.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: it's maximum employment and it's still more or less nearly there at 4.2%.
claims.claim: Because labour supply and demand are both shrinking, the unemployment rate stays near 4.2% even as job growth and demand weaken, which keeps the Fed's mandate gauge from signalling urgency and makes the policy choice hard.
claims.indicator: unemployment rate, labour force participation, payroll growth
claims.conditions: Immigration cuts keep unemployment low despite weak demand.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: the unemployment rate is probably the most important number that they watch.
claims.claim: The Fed treats the unemployment rate as its most important labour indicator, which simplifies its reaction function despite GDP/income mismeasurement.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: what we're looking at from a cyclical perspective is the changes kind of month to month, quarter to quarter, which shouldn't be overly impacted by those kind of structural trends.
claims.claim: Structural mismeasurement of a digital services economy matters less for month-to-month changes, so cyclical signals built on changes remain usable.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the changes you see in unemployment among really young people in certain um I think it was college graduates uh young college graduates was was really increasing a lot at the moment
claims.claim: Rising unemployment among young college graduates (citing Jim) is an early sign of AI's labour effect that headline GDP/employment data do not yet show.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: you've had mandates drift at the Fed as well you know because they started talking about climate change
claims.claim: Critics from the hard-money side say the Fed missed the 2021 inflation surge and drifted from its mandate (climate, inclusive employment), and Bessent and Warsh call for root-and-branch reform, so institutional change at the Fed is a live risk.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: Worsh isn't a trained economist either. So he's more of a I mean he's probably more of a political mover.
claims.claim: Recent Fed chairs (Powell, and candidate Warsh) are not academic economists, so the appointee is more of a political actor and Fed policy more exposed to political aims.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Vulkar specifically told Congress that they had to cut deficit and and that's a very important uh point to leave out I think
claims.claim: Warsh cites Volcker but omits that Volcker demanded deficit cuts from Congress; a hard-money Fed that stops financing deficits without fiscal action is incomplete.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that the pandemic and the Ukraine war had anything to do with the inflation that came. Uh it was all down to the Fed.
claims.claim: Warsh attributes the 2021 inflation entirely to the Fed and denies supply-shock effects; Niels agrees the Fed was out of touch but says supply issues mattered.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: but they're being put in charge to kind of solve the problem, but if you have your own positions in one way, how how likely are you going to go against that?
claims.claim: Conflict of interest: hedge-fund titans who expect higher rates from the deficit are being given policy influence while holding positions, so incentives may favour not solving the problem.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: in theory that would push up bond yields and and kind of naturally force the administration to do something
claims.claim: If a Warsh Fed stopped financing the deficit, bond yields would rise and force fiscal action in theory, but the administration has had the chance on the deficit and has not acted, so this is a potential stress point.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: bestinance philosophy seems to be to try and grow your way out of the deficit. Um whether that's achievable or not who knows probably seems seems um optimistic.
claims.claim: Bessent's strategy is to grow out of the deficit with deregulation, which looks optimistic given entitlement spending and the new spending bill.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: The trend index up 10 basis points but still down just shy of 10% for the year.
claims.claim: At 5 August 2025 CTA indices were still negative year to date (Beta 50 -3.93%, SG CTA -7.76%, SG Trend about -10%, Short Term Traders about -6%) while MSCI World was +11.7%, the S&P 500 +8.7% and aggregate bonds +4.5%.
claims.indicator: SG Trend, SG CTA, BTOP50, MSCI World, S&P 500 YTD

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: managers that maybe had out had out had outperformed a little bit maybe by being a bit slower um had uh had lagged a bit
claims.claim: On the last day of July, slower managers that had outperformed lagged while underperformers recovered; faster and medium-term trend models have struggled in 2025 and longer-term trend has been paid, worth monitoring.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: their aum has been growing. They've had very strong inflows but their fees have been going down because of not being in performance fees
claims.claim: Man Group's AUM and inflows are growing, but fee income fell because trend funds earned no performance fees; its executives call it one of the toughest periods in 25 to 30 years while saying trend following is not broken.
claims.indicator: Man Group AUM and fee income

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the case for trend following hasn't changed, but the burden of patient has gone up.
claims.claim: The economic case for trend following is unchanged but investors must now tolerate longer drawdowns, i.e. the cost is behavioural patience.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: back in 2019 I heard plenty of people telling me oh you know trend following is not going to work anymore. Central banks manipulate markets and they they dampen the volume.
claims.claim: In 2019 many said central banks had dampened volatility so trends were dead, yet trend performed well in 2021-22 for three to four years: such 'it's over' narratives are cyclical and unreliable.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think it's been a 14 15 month period that's been challenging the draw down is nothing bigger than what it's been before
claims.claim: Niels disputes the 'three bad years' story: trend has had a 14 to 15 month challenging period with a drawdown not larger than earlier ones, caused by simultaneous reversals in several big sectors plus political noise driving V-shaped equity sell-offs.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: I think it had the sharp for the uh liquid diversifiers historically at 0.44
claims.claim: In AQR's study the liquid diversifier (trend) had a historical Sharpe of 0.44; the forward-looking analysis assumed lower but still supported the same result.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: but they're survivors so you know you know sure they live through it right.
claims.claim: Using managers that lived through the 1970s as a proxy suffers survivorship bias, which is why AQR backfills with discounted indices instead.

claims.speaker: Alan (co-host, Dublin-based allocator; surname garbled in captions)
claims.quote: it seems pessimistic on the return assumptions for equities and a bit more optimistic maybe on return assumptions for liquid diversifiers.
claims.claim: AQR's conclusion rests on pessimistic equity return assumptions and relatively optimistic diversifier return assumptions, so the case depends on one's beliefs on expected returns.
